case_name: Lalonde v Sena Solid Waste Holdings Inc
text:
Court of Queen’s Bench of Alberta

Citation: Lalonde
v Sena Solid Waste Holdings Inc, 2017 ABQB 374

Date:
20170613

Docket:
1303 01585

Registry:
Edmonton

Between:

Kerry Lalonde

Plaintiff

- and -

Sena Solid Waste Holdings Inc.

Defendant

Corrected judgment:
A corrigendum was issued on June 19,
2017; the corrections have been made to the text and the corrigendum is
appended to this judgment.

_______________________________________________________

Reasons for Judgment

of the

Honourable Mr. Justice

J.J.
Gill

_______________________________________________________

Introduction

[
1
]

This is an employment law matter. The plaintiff
was dismissed without cause. The issue to be decided is what amounts are owing
to the plaintiff as a result of his wrongful dismissal.

Background

[
2
]

Mr. Lalonde (“the Plaintiff”) is a 62 year old Millwright.
He received his Journeyman Millwright Certificate in 1991. His career includes
working as a contractor with his own oilfield service company from 1980 to
2004.

[
3
]

In March 2007, he started working as a contract
employee at the Swan Hills Waste Treatment Plant (“the facility”) which is
operated by SENA Solid Waste Holdings Inc. (“the Defendant”). On April 15
th
,
2008, after being invited to join the company by a manager of the Defendant, he
became a full time employee of the Defendant as a Journeyman Millwright,
Technician 111 in the Maintenance Department.

[
4
]

The Plaintiff signed a letter of employment
(“the April, 2008 employment letter”). When ownership of the facility changed
he signed another letter of employment on February 24th, 2011 (“the February, 2011
employment letter”).

[
5
]

The Plaintiff worked continuously at the facility
from April 15, 2008 until his dismissal on July 24th, 2012. The Plaintiff
expected to work at the facility until it closed in December 2015. He assumed
that if he did a good job he would be allowed to stay until the facility
closed. There is no evidence the Defendant advised him that he would be
employed until the facility closed.

[
6
]

Prior to his dismissal in July 2012, the
Plaintiff had not received any verbal or written warnings or been subject to
any suspensions. In April 2012 he received a letter advising him that he had
earned a merit increase and his “
hard work and efforts contributed to our
overall solid performance and we want to thank you
” [Emphasis added].

[
7
]

The Plaintiff’s compensation included a short-term
and long-term retention initiative payment. Under the terms of the retention
initiative employees released without cause are entitled to compensation.

[
8
]

The events leading to his suspension and
ultimate dismissal took place on June 13, 2012. That work day started as usual
with a tailgate meeting of about eight maintenance staff including the
Plaintiff, his supervisor Derrick Nelson, and a contract worker called Adrian.
The Plaintiff advised his supervisor he was going to do preventive maintenance
that day.

[
9
]

After leaving the tailgate meeting, the Plaintiff
went to the maintenance shop and obtained a work permit to cover the work he
was about to do. Obtaining a work permit was standard practice. Midmorning he
went to the control room. Adrian came in and asked him a question about the RBR
unit and the Plaintiff provided him with some information.

[
10
]

Later that morning the Plaintiff spoke with the
Safety Supervisor, Mark Rosenberger who inquired about Adrian. He wanted to
know if Adrian had a permit. The Plaintiff did

not know and nothing else
was said. The Plaintiff then finished some paperwork and went for lunch.

[
11
]

After lunch the Plaintiff picked up another
permit to do work in another area of the facility. Later in the afternoon he was
called by radio to a meeting at the office of the Maintenance Manager, Victor
Goegan.

[
12
]

Mr. Goegan told him to sit down and then
proceeded to accuse him of a number of workplace infractions. The Plaintiff
described the conversation as Victor “chewing him out a new one.” He was
accused of putting a life in danger and of insubordination. The allegation of
putting a life in danger related to Adrian who apparently was working without a
permit. The allegation of insubordination related to the Plaintiff’s alleged
failure to follow his supervisor’s direction concerning the disposal of scrap
metal. The Plaintiff was also accused of lying to his supervisor in relation to
the scrap metal.

[
13
]

The Plaintiff was surprised by the criticism. He
tried to respond to the allegations but was given little, if any, opportunity
to do so. He tried to convey the fact that it was his supervisor’s
responsibility (not his) to assign work to Adrian. The Plaintiff was suspended and
summarily escorted off the facility by two other employees.

[
14
]

Subsequent to his suspension the Plaintiff made
several unsuccessful efforts to communicate his side of the story including
writing to and phoning Mr. Goegan.

[
15
]

After his suspension the Plaintiff heard nothing
from the Defendant for several weeks. The Plaintiff testified that the period
of time while suspended and waiting for a response or update from the Defendant
was difficult. He found it very stressful. After meeting with his doctor he
went on stress leave. Two letters from his doctor were entered at trial. They
indicate that he was unable to work from July 3, 2012 to July 20, 2012.

[
16
]

The Defendant never responded to the Plaintiff’s
request for more information. The record shows that the
Defendant was aware that the Plaintiff was under stress. An internal email
written by Mr. Goegan commented that the Plaintiff had called and “he’s a bit
stressed.”

[
17
]

On July 24, 2012 the Plaintiff received a letter
from the Defendant which advised him that his employment had been terminated.
The first paragraph states as follows: “This letter confirms your employment
with SENA Waste Services will end effective July 24, 2012. After which you will
no longer be considered an active employee. You’re being terminated with cause
due to your of failure to follow safety procedures and your failure to follow
your supervisor’s instructions.”

[
18
]

On July 26, 2012 the Plaintiff wrote in what he
described “as a last resort” to Philip Allouche, a Division Manager with the Defendant.
In that letter he provides a detailed response to the allegations and asks a number
of questions.

[
19
]

On August 17, 2012 he received an email from the
Defendant’s Human Resources Manager, Yvonne Bur. In that email, which was
copied to a number of other senior employees, Ms. Bur states:

During our investigations, we identified the
following:

(a)

Failure to meet your Employee Responsibilities as per Section 3.1 of
the SHTC Safety Manual which reads: “Take reasonable care to protect the health
and safety of himself/herself and other workers in Corporation with the
employer.”

(b)

Failure to follow Safe Work Procedures as per Section
17.1 of the SHTC Safety Manual and obtain a Work Permit.

(c)

Failure to follow Incident Reporting Procedures
as per Section 13.3 of the SHTC Safety Manual and report any incidents
immediately to your immediate Supervisor or his/her delegate.

(d)

Failure to follow your Supervisor instructions
that scrap steel/metal was only to be discarded in the large “Maple Leaf Bins.”

[
20
]

The Plaintiff issued a Statement of Claim
seeking compensation for his wrongful dismissal and the Defendant filed a
lengthy Statement of Defence outlining in detail the alleged cause for the
dismissal.

[
21
]

In May 2017, on the opening day of trial, the Defendant
withdrew the allegations of cause.

[
22
]

At trial the Plaintiff was asked to respond to
the original allegations made by the Defendant. Firstly, in relation to the
allegation that he failed to protect the safety of an employee, he was not
advised at the tailgate meeting that he was responsible for supervising Adrian.
He did not know that Adrian did not have a permit. He was told after the fact
but had no knowledge of this in advance.

[
23
]

The Plaintiff’s evidence is confirmed by a
letter entered at trial from another employee (Larry Dakin) dated July 10, 2012
who was present at the tailgate meeting. In that letter, which was addressed to
the Defendant, Mr. Dakin indicates there was no mention at the tailgate meeting
of the Plaintiff being responsible for or in charge of Adrian. In fact, Mr.
Dakin recalled that when the Plaintiff was asked what he was doing that day, he
indicated he was going to be doing preventive maintenance.

[
24
]

Secondly, the Plaintiff was essentially accused of
insubordination for not following or ignoring the specific direction from his
supervisor concerning storage of scrap metal.

[
25
]

The Plaintiff described a number of the
employees discussing moving specialty metal into scrap bins and recycling it.
Any monies earned would be for the social club.

[
26
]

The Plaintiff had asked Don Freckleton, the
Plant Manager, if they could do this and he said he would think about it. Scrap
metal was collected and put in bins. Subsequently, his supervisor decided to
clean up the warehouse and dumped those bins into a large scrap bin. The
Plaintiff testified that he did not object and did not ignore or disobey any
directions from his supervisor.

[
27
]

After being dismissed the Plaintiff applied for
EI benefits. However, as a result of being terminated for cause his EI was
delayed for 6 to 8 weeks. The Plaintiff was able to find another job after a
few months. He was not able to find another job as a millwright.

[
28
]

A letter from the Plaintiff’s wife Rena Lalonde
was entered as an exhibit. It describes the negative impacts that the dismissal
had on the Plaintiff. The impacts included a change in his personality and a
loss of interest in family and other matters. Ms. Lalonde believes that the
worst part for the Plaintiff was the humiliation he suffered while being
escorted off the facility followed by the treatment he received from SENA
Management and the HR department in the weeks that followed his dismissal. She
described the Plaintiff as being depressed, miserable, isolated and angry. She
believes he has mental health problems and has not recovered from the firing. In
the letter Ms. Lalonde mentions an incident when the Plaintiff was told that the
general consensus around the plant was “Lalonde got fired because he was
stealing.”

[
29
]

The Plaintiff testified that the dismissal
caused him a lot of stress and has had a negative impact on his life.

Issues

1)

Do the employment letters signed by the Plaintiff limit the amount
of notice the Plaintiff is entitled to? What is the appropriate reasonable
notice period?

2)

Is the Plaintiff entitled to aggravated damages?

3)

Is the Plaintiff entitled to punitive damages?

Analysis

1) Do the employment letters signed by the Plaintiff limit
the amount of notice the Plaintiff is entitled to? What is the appropriate
reasonable notice period?

The employment letters

[
30
]

As noted above the Plaintiff signed the April,
2008 employment letter. When ownership of the facility changed in 2011 he also
signed the February, 2011 employment letter.

[
31
]

The Defendant submits that the wording of the April,
2008 employment letter limits the Plaintiff’s reasonable notice period to the
notice period prescribed by provincial legislation. That is, the Plaintiff is
entitled to only four weeks’ pay in lieu of notice under the
Employment
Standards Code
, RSA 2000, c E-9 (“the Code”).

[
32
]

In his submissions the Plaintiff suggests the February,
2011 employment letter is the relevant letter of employment. He submits that
the termination clause in that letter does not restrict the Plaintiff to the
notice period provided for under ss 56 and 57 of the
Code
. As a result,
the Plaintiff is entitled to any civil remedy available by law pursuant to s
3(1) of the
Code
.

[
33
]

The first issue to be decided is which
employment letter (the April 2008 letter or the February 2011 letter) applies?

[
34
]

I find that the April 2008 employment letter is
the applicable letter of employment. The Defendant has accepted that the
Plaintiff was employed since April 20, 2008 and is not asserting that the
February 2011 employment letter effectively restarted the Plaintiff’s
employment effective April 1, 2011. If I am wrong on that issue, it does not
affect the outcome as I agree with the Plaintiff’s interpretation that the
wording of the February, 2011 employment letter does not limit the Plaintiff’s
notice to the amount prescribed by provincial legislation.

[
35
]

Turning to the April 2008 employment letter, it
includes the following “Termination” provision:

Should your employment with Earth Tech
Canada Inc. be terminated for any reason, other than willful or professional
misconduct, conflict of interest, disobedience or willful neglect of duty, that
has not been condoned by Earth Tech Canada Inc., your sole legal entitlement
will be notice of termination (or termination pay) and/or severance pay
equivalent to the legal requirements, as prescribed by provincial legislation,
and you will not be entitled to any payment in excess thereof.

[
36
]

The clause distinguishes between different types
of reasons for termination. Any reason (i.e. “other than willful or
professional misconduct, conflict of interest, disobedience or willful neglect
of duty, that has not been condoned by Earth Tech Canada Inc.”) will limit
entitlement to the amounts prescribed by provincial legislation. By
implication, if the reason is “willful or professional misconduct, conflict of
interest, disobedience or willful neglect of duty, that has not been condoned by
Earth Tech Canada Inc.” an employee’s entitlement is not limited to the amounts
prescribed by provincial legislation.

[
37
]

The Plaintiff was dismissed for alleged disobedience
and professional misconduct. Consequently, the April 2008 employment letter
signed by the Plaintiff does not limit the amount of notice the Plaintiff is
entitled to be paid.

What is the appropriate reasonable
notice period?

Positions of the parties

[
38
]

The Plaintiff submits that he was induced to
leave secure employment to work for the Defendant and expected his employment
to be of a permanent, full-time character until the facility was shut down December
31st, 2015. At the time of his termination he was a 56 year old senior
millwright, in a very responsible and technical position. Since his wrongful
termination, he has not been able to find similar alternative employment. In
addition, based on the bad faith actions of the Defendant, the Plaintiff has
failed to generate interviews to positions to which he is eminently qualified for
and has been forced to take a punishing labour-intensive position.

[
39
]

In terms of damages and reasonable notice
period, the Plaintiff in essence seeks approximately 18 months of lost income
minus the amounts he has earned as mitigation during this period. In addition,
he seeks lost RRSP contributions and retention initiatives. He seeks short term
retention initiatives amounts for the years 2012-2015 totalling $81,501.00 and
a long term retention initiative of $57, 841.00.

[
40
]

The Plaintiff refers to a number of cases including

Bardal v Globe & Mail Ltd
(1960),

1960 CanLII 294 (ON HCJ)
, 24 DLR (2d) 140 [“Bardal”] and
Wallace
v United Grain Growers Ltd
,
1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)
, [1997] 3 SCR 701.

[
41
]

The Defendant submits that if the notice period
is not determined through the employment letters the case law indicates that reasonable notice is based on
conventional factors such as age, length of service, degree of responsibility,
etc. Based on these factors the
Plaintiff should receive approximately 4 months’ notice.

[
42
]

The Defendant also notes that the Plaintiff
successfully mitigated his damages by obtaining employment in mid-October of
2012 earning $40/hr instead of the $42/hr he was earning with the Defendant.
The Defendant submits that the amount of reasonable notice should be set at $43, 819.26 less any
mitigation earned from July 24th, 2012 to November 24th, 2012.

[
43
]

In the alternative, the Defendant submits that if
the court finds five months’ reasonable notice is owed, the Defendant accepts
the calculation of the Plaintiff in his Schedule A that the shortfall was $29, 474 to the end of
2012.

Analysis

[
44
]

In
Wallace v United Grains Ltd,

1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)
, [1997] 3 SCR 701, the Supreme Court addressed the issue of how to determine the
period of reasonable notice. At paragraph 116:

To determine the period of reasonable
notice, the court examines the characteristics of the particular employment
relationship relevant to the employee’s prospects of finding a similar position
including “the character of the employment, the length of service of the
servant, the age of the servant and the availability of similar employment,
having regard to the experience, training and qualifications of the servant”:
Bardal
v Globe & Mail Ltd
.

[
45
]

At paragraph 82 the Supreme Court also noted
that the
Bardal
case does not state, nor has it been interpreted
to imply, that the factors enumerated in that case were exhaustive.

[
46
]

In
Nelson v Champion Feed Services Inc.
,
2010
abqb
409 at paras 86-87,
Justice Graesser summarized the law in relation to what is reasonable notice:

No two cases are identical. And there is no
set formula that is to be applied.
Bardal v Globe & Mail Ltd.

(1960),
1960 CanLII 294 (ON HCJ)
, 24 D.L.R. (2d) 140 (Ont. H.C.) at p. 145 (confirmed in
Wallace v
United Grain Growers Ltd
.,
1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)
, [1997] 3 S.C.R. 701 (S.C.C.)) gives
instruction as to the calculation of the appropriate notice period. It required
an analysis of a number of factors in the context of determining how long it is
likely to take this employee to find suitable alternate employment. The
analysis is performed prospectively, at the time of the dismissal, rather than
retrospectively at the time of trial. The length of time it actually takes the
dismissed employee to find suitable alternate employment may be a relevant
consideration, but is not determinative.

The [
Bardal
]
factors are:

1.

The nature of the employment – the more senior
the position, the longer it is likely to take to find a replacement position.
There are fewer senior management jobs around.

2.

The length of service – the longer an employee
has worked for one employer, the more difficult it may be to find an alternate
job. Either because the employee has narrowed his or her skills by working for
one employer for a long time, or the employee has been paid more than the job
is worth because of long service.

3.

The age of the employee – the older the employee
is, the less likely he or she is to find a suitable position, or the longer it
is likely to take. Older employees are sometimes perceived as less worthwhile
to invest in.

4.

The availability of suitable similar employment
having regard to the employee’s experience, training and qualifications
together with surrounding economic circumstances – what is the realistic
prospect of this employee getting a similar replacement job? What is the job
market like? In good economic times, jobs may be plentiful and the employee may
have little difficulty finding a good replacement job; in poorer times, there
may be few jobs around.

[
47
]

The Plaintiff was employed continuously from
April 2008 to his termination in July 2012 being a period of just over 4 years.
I am not satisfied that the evidence supports a finding that he was enticed or
induced to leave secure employment to work for the Defendant nor that there was
any representation that this would be a permanent, full-time job until the
facility was shut down on December 31, 2015.

[
48
]

At the time of his dismissal the Plaintiff was a
56 year old millwright. Clearly he occupied a responsible and technical position
with the Defendant. On occasion he was required to supervise other workers
(including contract workers).

[
49
]

The evidence is that shortly after his dismissal
he obtained employment earning close to the hourly wage he was earning with the
Defendant but the overall quality of the new employment was lower. He is now
required to drive long distances to different job sites and the work is more
physically challenging.

[
50
]

He had difficulty finding similar employment as
a millwright and despite applying for many jobs for which he appeared to be
eminently qualified for he has been unsuccessful in obtaining similar
employment. It is impossible to know precisely why but it is a reasonable
inference from the evidence that the difficulty in obtaining similar quality
employment is related to a number of factors including his age, the surrounding
economic circumstances, and the circumstances surrounding his dismissal. I will
discuss this in more detail under the heading of aggravated damages.

[
51
]

I have reviewed the case law on the subject of
reasonable notice provided by the parties. None of the cases are that similar
to the facts of this case. The most relevant cases are the following:
Meyer
v Danka Business Systems Ltd
,
2001 BCSC 428
(55-year-old senior
salesperson with 4 years of service received 10 months’ notice);
Ghate v
Acres Consulting Services Ltd
,

1986 CarswellOnt 855
(50-year-old
engineer with 4 years for service received 10 months’ notice);
Humble v
Atlantic Rentals Ltd
,
2004 NBQB 362
(53-year-old heavy equipment
operator with close to 8 years of service received 8 months’ notice;
Stancu
v ECE Group Ltd
,
[2005] OJ No 4277
(59-year-old CAD operator
with two and half years of service received 4 months’ notice).

[
52
]

I find a reasonable notice period to be in the
range of 4 to 8 months taking into account: the length of the Plaintiff’s
employment (less than 5 years), his age at dismissal (56), the nature of his
employment (tradesman doing fairly technical work, with occasional, minor
supervisory responsibilities) and the availability of similar work. I set the
notice period at 6 months.

[
53
]

In calculating the amounts owing for this notice
period there is an additional component to his compensation being the retention
initiative bonus.

[
54
]

In the case of
Paquette v TeraGo Networks
Inc.
,
2016 ONCA 618
the court considered whether the plaintiff was
entitled to certain bonuses as part of a wrongful dismissal. The law
surrounding entitlement to bonuses, in the absence of an agreement, was summarized
as follows (at paras 16-17):

The basic principle in awarding damages for
wrongful dismissal is that the terminated employee is entitled to compensation
for all losses arising from the employer's breach of contract in failing to
give proper notice. The damages award should place the employee in the same
financial position he or she would have been in had such notice been given:
Sylvester
v. British Columbia
,
1997 CanLII 353 (SCC)
,
[1997] 2 S.C.R. 315

(S.C.C.), at para.
1
. In other words, in determining damages for wrongful
dismissal, the court will typically include all of the compensation and
benefits that the employee would have earned during the notice period:
Davidson
v. Allelix Inc

(1991),
1991 CanLII 7091 (ON CA)
,
7 O.R. (3d) 581

(Ont. C.A.), at para.
21
.

Damages for wrongful dismissal may include
an amount for a bonus the employee would have received had he continued in his
employment during the notice period, or damages for the lost opportunity to
earn a bonus. This is generally the case where the bonus is an integral part of
the employee's compensation package: see
Brock v. Matthews Group Ltd
.

(1988),
20 C.C.E.L. 110
(Ont. H.C.), at para. 44
, aff'd
(1991),
34 C.C.E.L. 50
(Ont. C.A.), at paras. 6-7
(appeal allowed
in part on other grounds);
Bernier
, at
para. 44 (Ont. S.C.), aff'd, at para. 5 (Ont. C.A.). This can be the case even
where a bonus is described as "discretionary": see
Brock v. Matthews Group Ltd
,
at para. 44 (Ont. H.C.J.), aff'd, at paras. 6-7 (Ont.
C.A.).

[
55
]

In addition to his monthly salary, the Plaintiff
is also entitled to a portion of the retention initiative that he would have
earned during this notice period. The retention initiative expressly outlines
how the bonus will be paid upon dismissal. It states as follows: “employees who
are released without cause will be compensated on a pro-rated basis under the
Short Term Initiative and under the Long Term Initiative. Any pro-rated
payments will be based on the number of months worked in the calendar year with
one day worked in a month being considered working in that month.”

[
56
]

Damages for the loss of this retention bonus in
the amount of 6 months should be added to the 6 months of salary. Any income earned
during this period as mitigation should be deducted.

3.         Is the Plaintiff entitled to aggravated
damages?

Positions of the parties

[
57
]

The Plaintiff submits that he is entitled to
aggravated damages as a result of how he was treated by his employer before and
during the termination.

[
58
]

The Plaintiff contends he was essentially accused
of theft of company property. The theft allegations were a main factor for his
termination as is evident in the Defendant’s Statement of Defence. He was
humiliated when escorted off company property in full view of his co-workers. The
Defendant did not rescind their position that he was terminated for just cause
until the eve of trial.

[
59
]

The Plaintiff submits that in the five years
since termination his employment prospects were hamstrung by the Defendant’s
spurious allegations. The Plaintiff notes he resides in a small community and
because of the allegations he was unable to secure similar alternative
employment due to the rumors surrounding his termination. He believes his
previously good reputation was and continues to be harmed by the Defendant’s
bad faith conduct.

[
60
]

In addition, the Plaintiff points to what he
submits is a one sided investigation undertaken by the Defendant prior to his
termination. At no point were the Plaintiff’s concerns addressed and he was not
able to provide, what is now conceded by the Defendant, to be the true version
of the events.

[
61
]

The Plaintiff points also to his wife’s letter
which was entered as evidence. In that letter she indicates that the
termination greatly affected their relationship. She indicates the Plaintiff is
now depressed, miserable and uninterested in activities and relationships with
family members that he previously relished. She notes that the physical
laborious work he has been forced into as a result of his termination has
caused a great deal of economic, physical and mental stress. She believes but
for the conduct of the Defendant, the Plaintiff’s reputation and positive
familial relationships would have likely remained intact.

[
62
]

The Defendant submits there is no basis for an
award of aggravated damages. It is admitted that aggravated damages can only be
awarded for actual damages provided the employee can prove that the manner of
dismissal caused mental distress that was in contemplation of the parties. The
Defendant suggests that the Plaintiff has not demonstrated any damages
resulting from the matter of his dismissal.

[
63
]

The Defendant notes, in this case, they had
conducted an investigation and suspended the Plaintiff with pay during that time.
The Defendant interviewed many people and certainly had evidence to conclude
the Plaintiff had breached a safety rule and had been insubordinate. Therefore,
the conduct of the Defendant does not meet the requirements for bad faith as
set out in the case law.

[
64
]

The Defendant denies that there was any
allegation of theft. The reasons for dismissal were breach of safety rules and
insubordination. The Defendant suggests that no weight should be given to the
letter written by Mrs. Lalonde.

[
65
]

In addition, the Defendant suggests that there
is no evidence that it committed any malicious or outrageous acts, either
through the investigation or the dismissal on the part of the Defendant. The
facts in this case are very different from the cases relied upon by the
Plaintiff. In
Boucher v Wal-Mart Canada Corp,

2014 ONCA 419
an
individual was terrorized by her employer for years for failing to agree to do
something fraudulent. Similarly in

Karmel v Calgary Jewish Academy
,

2015 ABQB 731
the employee was terrorized for a lengthy period of time.

Analysis

[
66
]

One can characterize what happened here as a
case where the Defendant decided to “shoot first and ask questions later.” It
is unclear why the Defendant maintained, what they now readily agree, were
unsubstantiated allegations for so many years.

[
67
]

The Defendant suggests that its actions
throughout were appropriate. It points to the investigation that was undertaken
to determine whether the Plaintiff should be dismissed. However, clearly
missing from that investigation was any serious consideration of the Plaintiff’s
side of the story. I find that the Plaintiff was never given a proper
opportunity to present his side of the story both prior to being suspended and
prior to being fired.

[
68
]

The evidence suggests that the Defendant had
made up his mind to dismiss the Plaintiff within days of his suspension,
therefore supporting the conclusion that the investigation was at best
incompetent and unfair and at worst a sham. The Defendant clearly ignored or
failed to give proper weight to information it received from another employee
(Larry Dakin) who was present at the tailgate meeting on June 13, 2012. Mr.
Dakin supported the Plaintiff’s account of what happened at the tailgate
meeting.

[
69
]

In
Keays v Honda Canada Inc,

2008
SCC 39
, the Supreme Court summarized the law surrounding damages that may result
from the manner of dismissal. Beginning at para 57:

Damages resulting from the manner of
dismissal must then be available only if they result from the circumstances
described in
Wallace
,
namely where the employer engages in conduct during the course of dismissal
that is "unfair or is in bad faith by being, for example, untruthful,
misleading or unduly insensitive" (para. 98).

The application of
Fidler
makes
it unnecessary to pursue an extended analysis of the scope of any implied duty
of good faith in an employment contract.
Fidler

provides that "as long as the promise in relation to state of mind is a
part of the bargain in the reasonable contemplation of the contracting parties,
mental distress damages arising from its breach are recoverable" (para.
48). In
Wallace
, the
Court held employers "to an obligation of good faith and fair dealing in
the manner of dismissal" (para. 95) and created the expectation that, in
the course of dismissal, employers would be "candid, reasonable, honest
and forthright with their employees" (para. 98). At least since that time,
then, there has been expectation by both parties to the contract that employers
will act in good faith in the manner of dismissal. Failure to do so can lead to
foreseeable, compensable damages. As aforementioned, this Court recognized as
much in
Fidler

itself,
where we noted that the principle in
Hadley

"explains
why an extended period of notice may have been awarded upon wrongful dismissal
in employment law" (para. 54).

To be perfectly clear, I will conclude this
analysis of our jurisprudence by saying that there is no reason to retain the
distinction between "true aggravated damages" resulting from a
separate cause of action and moral damages resulting from conduct in the manner
of termination. Damages attributable to conduct in the manner of dismissal are
always to be awarded under the
Hadley

principle.
Moreover, in cases where damages are awarded, no extension of the notice period
is to be used to determine the proper amount to be paid. The amount is to be
fixed according to the same principles and in the same way as in all other
cases dealing with moral damages. Thus, if the employee can prove that the
manner of dismissal caused mental distress that was in the contemplation of the
parties, those damages will be awarded not through an arbitrary extension of
the notice period, but through an award that reflects the actual damages.
Examples
of conduct in dismissal resulting in compensable damages are attacking the
employee's reputation by declarations made at the time of dismissal, misrepresentation
regarding the reason for the decision, or dismissal meant to deprive the
employee of a pension benefit or other right, permanent status for instance

(see also the examples in
Wallace
,

at paras.
99-100
) [Emphasis added].

[
70
]

The Alberta Court of Appeal considered the issue
of aggravated damages in
Elgert  v Home Hardware Stores

Ltd,

2011 ABCA 112
, though the court held at para 73:

Damages resulting from the
manner
of
dismissal (as opposed to the fact of dismissal) are available, however, if
damages arise out of the conduct of the employer in the course of termination.
To be compensable, such conduct must be unfair or in bad faith, in that it is “untruthful,
misleading or unduly insensitive.”

[
71
]

In
Wallace v United Grain Growers Ltd
,

1997 CanLII 332 (SCC)
, [1997] 3 SCR 701 the Supreme Court provided some examples of conduct that would
support an award of aggravated damages. Beginning at para 98:

The obligation of good faith and fair
dealing is incapable of precise definition. However, at a minimum, I believe
that in the course of dismissal employers ought to be candid, reasonable,
honest and forthright with their employees and should refrain from engaging in
conduct that is unfair or is in bad faith by being, for example, untruthful,
misleading or unduly insensitive. In order to illustrate possible breaches of
this obligation, I refer now to some examples of the conduct over which the
courts expressed their disapproval in the cases cited above.

In
Trask, supra
, an employer
maintained a wrongful accusation of involvement in a theft and communicated
this accusation to other potential employers of the dismissed employee.

Jivrag, supra
, involved similar unfounded accusations of
theft combined with a refusal to provide a letter of reference after the
termination, In
Dunning, supra
, bad faith conduct was clearly present.
Although the plaintiff’s position had been eliminated, he was told by several
senior executives that another position would probably be found for him and
that the new assignment would necessitate a transfer. However, at the same time
that the plaintiff was being reassured about his future, a senior
representative of the company was contemplating his termination. When a
position could not be found, the decision was made to terminate the plaintiff.
This decision was not communicated to the plaintiff for over a month despite
the fact that his employers knew he was in a process of selling his home in
anticipation of the transfer. News of his termination was communicated to the
plaintiff abruptly following the sale of his home [Emphasis added].

[
72
]

In this case, I am satisfied that the actions of
the Defendant amount to a breach of the obligation of good faith and fair
dealing and support an award of aggravated damages. Those actions include the
following:

1)

The Plaintiff was summarily terminated after
being accused of serious safety violations and insubordination relating to
alleged retention of salvageable equipment and scrap metal and failure to
supervise an unassigned contract worker.

2)

The Defendant maintained these allegations which
are described in the Statement of Defence as “serious safety violations and
insubordination” from the date of suspension in June, 2012 until shortly before
trial in May 2017 at which time they withdrew those allegations.

3)

Two days after the Plaintiff’s suspension,
without regard for his explanation and without giving him an opportunity to
fully explain the alleged misconduct, a decision was made to terminate his
employment on the 15
th
of June. An internal memo from the
Maintenance Manager, Mr. Goegan, to the HR Manager, Ms. Burr, shows a decision
had been made to terminate the Plaintiff; this despite not having any response
from the Plaintiff as to the alleged breaches of conduct. The Defendant ignored
a letter from an employee (Larry Dakin) which supported the Plaintiff’s
contention that he had done nothing wrong in relation to the alleged lack of
supervision of a contract employee. The evidence supports the conclusion that
the internal investigation was essentially a sham.

4)

The nature of the allegation concerning the
mishandling of salvageable equipment and scrap metal implied some form of
illegal conduct or dishonesty on the part of the Plaintiff. This suggestion can
be found in the Statement of Defence where the Defendant outlined in detail the
alleged cause for termination using such wording as “the plaintiff’s serious
safety violations and insubordination.” The Statement of Defence suggested that
the dismissal for cause included “unsatisfactory performance, dishonesty,
insubordination, serious misconduct.” In the Statement of Defence the
Plaintiff’s misconduct is described as constituting “serious misconduct,
insubordination and conduct constituting cause.” It is stated that “the
Plaintiff’s misconduct was such that it interfered with and prejudiced the safe
and proper conduct of the SHTC thereby, justifying cause for immediate
dismissal.”

[
73
]

Other examples include paragraph 36 in the
Statement of Defence which indicates that the Defendant “could not justify
continued employment of the Plaintiff given his cavalier attitude toward safety
and clear lack of respect for his Supervisor’s authority” [Emphasis added].

[
74
]

Paragraph 37 states:

The conduct of the Plaintiff constitutes:

a)

Breach of express or implied terms of the Plaintiff’s Employment
Agreement;

b)

Breach of express or implied terms of the
Plaintiff’s Agreement to abide and be bound by SHTC’s Safety Manual and its
Safety Policies and Procedures;

c)

Disregard for his safety, the safety of his
coworkers and the community;

d)

Insubordination; and;

e)

Incompetence or negligence.

[
75
]

I note also that there was evidence of the
impact that the actions of the Defendant, before and at the time of dismissal,
has had on the Plaintiff. I note that while the evidence from the Plaintiff’s
wife was in letter form it was not contradicted and was supported in substance
by the sworn evidence of the Plaintiff. As already discussed, the letter
describes how the termination has greatly affected their relationship and how
the Plaintiff is now depressed, miserable and uninterested in activities and
relationships with family members that he previously relished. She explains the
economic, physical and mental stress that he had gone through. In addition, his
reputation has suffered. I note also, that the Plaintiff lives in a small town,
and the Defendant was one of the larger employers located close to the small
community where the Plaintiff lived and it is reasonable to infer that the
information concerning his termination and the ongoing allegations may have had
an effect on both his reputation in the community and also his ability to
obtain similar work due to the rumors surrounding his termination.

[
76
]

I note also that the Plaintiff’s EI benefits
were delayed as a result of the allegations of cause made by the Defendant at
the time of the dismissal.

[
77
]

In summary, I am satisfied that the Defendant’s
conduct during the course of dismissal was unfair, breached the requirement of good
faith and the expectation that both parties to the contract had that the
employer would act in good faith in the manner of dismissal.

[
78
]

The Plaintiff has proven that the manner of
dismissal caused mental distress, particularly by the Defendant’s actions in
attacking the Plaintiff’s reputation at the time of dismissal and representing
that there was sufficient cause for dismissal for an extended period of time.

[
79
]

The Plaintiff seeks aggravated damages in the
amount of $125,000.00. Reviewing the case law relied upon by the Plaintiff,
including
Karmel v Calgary Jewish Academy
,
2015 ABQB 731

[“Karmel”] and
Boucher v Wal-Mart Canada Corp,

2014 ONCA 419

[“Boucher”], I find the amounts awarded in those cases to be inappropriate for
the facts of this case. In
Karmel
and
Boucher
the
actions of the employers were much more prolonged, serious and arguably
vindictive, thus in those cases the conduct

supported

a claim of
$200,000 in aggravated damages.

[
80
]

In this case there was abusive conduct leading
up to the dismissal, inappropriate and false reasons for dismissal and an
inadequate and unfair investigation. The plaintiff did not receive procedural
fairness. I would characterize the actions of the Defendant in this case to be
less serious and egregious than in both
Boucher
and
Karmel

thereby

warranting lower damages. Although the Defendants actions appear
not to have been vindictive, they were intentional, unnecessarily prolonged and
caused the Plaintiff significant mental distress. The wrongful allegations were
maintained for almost 5 years causing the Plaintiff considerable mental
distress during and after his sudden termination. He was publicly humiliated at
the time of dismissal and the humiliation continued as rumors concerning the
reasons he was dismissed continued to circulate. Consequently substantial
aggravated damages are justified for the Defendants failure to comply with their
duty to act in good faith.

[
81
]

It is difficult to quantify an award of
aggravated damages. No case is identical or directly applicable. The following
cases displayed similar unfair and insensitive conduct to what occurred in this
case.
Doyle v Zochem,
2016 ONSC 3188
,
aff’d
2017

ONCA
130
-
$60,000;
Strudwick v Applied Consumer & Clinical
Evaluations Inc,
2016 ONCA 520
-
$70,000;
Zesta
Engineering Ltd v Cloutier
(2010),
2010 ONSC 5810
,
additional
reasons

2013 ONSC 385
,
reversed in part on other grounds

2014
ONCA 762
-
$75,000;
Tim Ludwig Professional Corp v
BDO Canada LLP,
2017 ONCA 292
-
$100,000 aggravated
damages in a Partnership Context;
Price v 481530 BC Ltd,
2016
BCSC 1940
-
$50,000 aggravated damages;

Pate Estate v Galway-Cavendish and Harvey (Township),
2013
ONCA 669
–$100,000.
Taking into account the evidence in this case and the
jurisprudence, I award aggravated damages in the sum of $75,000.

4.         Is the Plaintiff entitled to punitive damages?

[
82
]

In addition, the Plaintiff submits that this is
an appropriate case to award punitive damages in order to deter future conduct
by the Defendant.

[
83
]

In support the Plaintiff refers to the conduct
of the Defendant’s manager, Mr. Goegan. In an email to another employee, Mr.
Goegan, shortly after the dismissal, made it clear that a decision to terminate
had been made without hearing from the Plaintiff. The Plaintiff submits that
the Defendant’s misconduct was a marked departure from the ordinary stance of
reasonable behaviour. It was malicious, oppressive and high handed. The
Plaintiff notes that in the month between the Plaintiff’s suspension and his
termination, he was kept in the dark regarding the Defendant’s plans. Even
though he had attempted to defend these spurious allegations against him, the
Defendant completed a one sided, high handed investigation.

[
84
]

The Defendant submits that there is no basis for
an award for punitive damages. There is no evidence that there was any
malicious or outrageous acts committed either through the investigation or the
dismissal on the part of the Defendant. The cases that are relied upon by the
Plaintiff involve situations that clearly exhibit malicious behaviour that
deserve punishment.

[
85
]

In
Ram v Michael Lacombe Group Inc
,

2017 BCSC 212
the court explains the differences between aggravated and punitive
damages at para 112:

While there may be some overlap in the facts
relevant to establishing each of these heads of damage, each rests upon a
different foundation and the purpose of awarding each is different. In a
wrongful dismissal case, aggravated damages are awarded to compensate a
plaintiff for actual damage that is caused by unfair or bad faith conduct of
the employer in the manner, as distinct from the fact, of the dismissal. In
contrast, the objects of punitive damages are retribution, deterrence and
denunciation as opposed to compensation, and punitive damages are restricted to
cases where an employer's conduct is so malicious and outrageous that it is
deserving of punishment:

Vernon v. British Columbia (Housing & Social
Development, Liquor Distribution Branch)
,
2012 BCSC 133
(B.C.
S.C.)
;
Rodrigues v. Shendon Enterprises Ltd
.
,
2010 BCSC 941
(B.C.
S.C.)
.

[
86
]

I agree with the Defendant that the actions of
the Defendant do not support an award of punitive damages. While the Defendant’s
actions were clearly insensitive, inappropriate and caused mental distress for
the Plaintiff, I do not find they were malicious.

[
87
]

The claim for punitive damages is dismissed.

Conclusion

[
88
]

In summary therefore, I find that the Plaintiff
is entitled to the following:

1)

An award of reasonable notice equivalent to 6
months’ salary and an allowance for missed Short Term and Long Term retention
bonuses. From this is deducted any monies earned in mitigation during the 6
month period.

2)

An award of aggravated damages of $75,000;

3)

Prejudgment interest pursuant to the
Judgment
Interest Act,
RSA 2000, c J-1 and amendments thereto.

4)

Costs.

[
89
]

If the parties cannot agree on costs, they may
contact me to make further representations.
